result: The authors generated and validated paramCherry flies by tagging the endogenous para locus with mCherry at the N-terminus. All Para isoforms (>60 generated by alternative splicing) share a common N-terminus and are tagged. The tagged flies are viable with mildly affected channel function, and ParamCherry localizes along CNS and PNS axons. Validation includes western blot showing molecular weight shift and immunohistochemistry confirming specificity.
evaluation: Claims C3-C10, C122-C123 provide converging evidence from multiple approaches (genetic tagging, western blot, immunohistochemistry, functional assays) that the paramCherry line is a valid tool for studying Para localization. The data show proper tagging, appropriate molecular weight, specific antibody detection, and minimal functional disruption.

result: Para and voltage-gated potassium channels show differential localization in larval neurons. Para localizes evenly along sensory axons but concentrates at the PNS/CNS boundary in motor axons. Shal co-localizes with Para in motor axons, while Shab resembles Para distribution in sensory axons. This suggests Drosophila motor axons have an AIS-like domain harboring both sodium and potassium channels.
evaluation: Claims C11-C16 are supported by cell-type-specific imaging using RNAi knockdown and endogenously tagged channels. The differential localization patterns are clearly demonstrated in Figures 2A-E, and the inference of an AIS-like domain (C16) is reasonable given the co-localization of Para and Shal at the motor axon boundary.

result: In adult flies, Para localizes to an AIS-like domain in motor neurons at the CNS/PNS boundary, while sensory neurons show even Para distribution along axons that fades in the neuropil. This pattern is demonstrated using FlpTag labeling and confirmed with anti-Para antibodies.
evaluation: Claims C17-C20 are supported by complementary approaches (FlpTag and antibody staining) showing consistent Para localization patterns in adult motor and sensory neurons (Figures 2F-I). The inference of an AIS in adult motor axons (C19) is reasonable given the localized Para enrichment.

result: Para channels are organized in clusters with regular spacing of approximately 0.6-0.8 μm along motor axons. This was demonstrated using high-resolution Airyscan microscopy, primary cell cultures, and super-resolution imaging of single motor axons. The clusters appear organized along lines at the motor axon.
evaluation: Claims C21-C25 are well-supported by multiple imaging approaches with consistent measurements (Figures 3A-G). The spacing measurements are quantified (0.620 μm by super-resolution, n=91 clusters) and replicated across different methods. The linear organization (C25) is supported by both light and electron microscopy.

result: In sensory neurons, Para shows low expression at the soma and distal axon, with increased localization at a distance from the soma, forming an AIS. Para also accumulates in distinct clusters within some dendrites. Para expression is weaker in sensory neurons than motor axons, and the motor axon AIS likely serves as a spike initiation zone with clustered Para channels.
evaluation: Claims C26-C32 are supported by FlpTag labeling of multidendritic sensory neurons (Figure 4). The localization patterns are clearly shown, though the authors note that lower expression prevented super-resolution analysis. The inference about spike initiation (C31) is supported by citation to computational modeling (Günay et al., 2015).

result: ParaApex2 insertion creates a weak hypomorphic allele that can be detected by electron microscopy. DAB precipitates show weak staining in small axons but intense staining in large axons near the CNS/PNS boundary. Serial sectioning reveals variable intensity suggesting clustered localization. 3D reconstruction shows ParaApex2 clusters organized in two lines along the axonal circumference with spacing of 0.706 μm.
evaluation: Claims C33-C39 are supported by electron microscopy data (Figure 5) with quantification. The functional characterization (C33) is shown in Figure 1B. The 3D reconstruction (C38) and spacing measurements (C39, n=54 distances) provide strong evidence for clustered organization consistent with light microscopy results.

result: Large caliber axons with high Para levels are embedded in a glial lacunar system characterized by intensive glial processes around axons >0.5 μm diameter. Glial processes average 35 nm thickness. The lacunar system is primarily formed by tract glia and positions Para channels close to a structure previously speculated to serve as an extracellular ion reservoir.
evaluation: Claims C40-C45 are supported by electron microscopy (Figures 5-6) with quantification (n=189 processes from 4 nerves, 3 animals). Apex2 labeling experiments (Figure 6A-B) confirm tract glia form the lacunae. The connection to ion reservoir function (C44-C45) is appropriately presented as inference supported by historical literature.

result: Adult leg nerves contain ~760 axons organized in zones by diameter. At the femur, large axons have single glial wraps while small axons are engulfed as fascicles. Near the CNS (coxa), large axons are flanked by up to 15 glial membrane sheets (~28 nm thick). Myelin-like structures increase at the distal end of lacunae but are absent near the neuropil.
evaluation: Claims C49-C56 are supported by extensive electron microscopy of leg nerves (Figure 7, supplementary figures) with quantification. Serial sectioning across 40-60 μm (Figure 7-supplement 2) provides spatial distribution data. The measurements are well-documented with sample sizes provided.

result: Both tract glia and peripheral wrapping glia can form myelin-like structures in leg nerves. These structures are generated by membrane folding rather than spiral growth, leaving axons incompletely insulated. Some areas show compaction with ~30 nm interperiodic distance (vs. 13 nm in mouse myelin). Unlike vertebrate myelin with MBP-mediated compaction, fly myelin shows only irregular extracellular space compaction, and MBP-like proteins are absent from the fly genome.
evaluation: Claims C57-C67 are supported by Apex2 labeling experiments and high-pressure freezing EM (Figure 7). The comparison to vertebrate myelin is appropriate with proper citations (C64-C65). The inference about MBP absence (C67) is based on genome knowledge. The structural characterization is thorough with multiple preparation methods.

result: Peripheral wrapping glia control Para localization and expression. Ablation of wrapping glia (but not ensheathing glia) causes redistribution of Para from concentrated at CNS/PNS boundary (2.5× enrichment) to even distribution along axons, plus a 2-fold increase in para mRNA. This loss of clustered distribution may contribute to reduced conductance velocity in glia-ablated animals.
evaluation: Claims C68-C77 are supported by glia ablation experiments with quantification (Figure 8C: n=10 larvae, p=0.0003; Figure 8D: n=7, p=0.0006). Controls show specificity to wrapping glia. The connection to conductance velocity (C77) is appropriately presented as inference supported by prior work (Kottmeier et al., 2020).

result: FGF-receptor manipulation in wrapping glia does not affect Para localization, suggesting that secreted proteins from wrapping glia might be needed for correct ion channel positioning.
evaluation: Claim C78 is supported by Figure 8-supplement 2F-H, but C79 is speculative. The negative result with FGF-receptor manipulation is informative but doesn't directly demonstrate that secreted proteins are responsible. Additional experiments would be needed to test this hypothesis.

result: In adults, the AIS-like domain is embedded in glial lacunae that may counteract ephaptic coupling and provide an ion reservoir. High Para expression is expected to generate ephaptic coupling forces that can synchronize but also interfere with neuronal signaling. The lacunar system spatially separates axons and provides extracellular space. Given tight membrane apposition (~20 nm) elsewhere, action potentials would rapidly deplete ions without a reservoir.
evaluation: Claims C80-C90 combine observational data (C80, C86, C88) with well-supported inferences about ephaptic coupling (C81-C84, properly cited) and ion reservoir function (C87, C89). The speculation about lacunar function (C85, C90) is reasonable given the structural data and is appropriately presented as hypothesis rather than established fact.

result: Myelin-like structures are found adjacent to lacunae, appearing to form from collapsed glial processes. These structures form at the distal end of lacunae (not lateral borders), suggesting insulation is not their primary function but rather they originate from lacunar collapse. Concomitantly, Para channel density decreases, reducing the need for an ion reservoir and favoring myelin formation.
evaluation: Claims C91-C97 are supported by serial section analysis (Figure 7-supplements 2-3) showing spatial relationships. The inferences about formation mechanism (C92, C95) and function (C94) are reasonable given the structural data. The correlation with Para density (C96-C97) is supported by EM observations, though the causal relationship is appropriately presented as inference.

result: Unlike vertebrate myelin with spiral growth, large fly nerves show membrane folding rather than spiral wrapping. However, spiral growth can be observed in small nerves with less extensive wrapping.
evaluation: Claims C98-C100 are supported by EM observations (Figure 7, supplements 4-5). The comparison to vertebrate myelin (C98) is appropriate as established knowledge. The structural differences are clearly documented in the images.

result: The evolution of myelin appears reflected in Drosophila development: (1) voltage-gated channels cluster at the AIS with glial help in larvae, (2) an ion reservoir (lacunar system) forms with increased channel expression in adults, and (3) glial process collapse in non-lacunar regions provides the basis for myelin formation.
evaluation: Claims C101-C104 synthesize the major findings into an evolutionary framework. C102 is well-supported by glia ablation data. C103-C104 are appropriately presented as inference/speculation based on the structural observations. This represents a reasonable interpretive model though direct evolutionary evidence is not provided.

result: The manuscript contextualizes findings within established knowledge about vertebrate and invertebrate nervous systems. Vertebrates use myelin and channel clustering for fast saltatory conduction, while invertebrates were thought to rely on radial growth with even channel distribution. Myelin-like structures exist in invertebrates but their relationship to channel distribution was unknown.
evaluation: Claims C105-C113 accurately represent established knowledge supported by appropriate citations. These provide important context for the novel findings. The statement about unknown relationships (C113) correctly identifies the knowledge gap addressed by this work.

result: In Drosophila larvae, peripheral axons are wrapped by single glial sheets resembling Remak fibers. Glia promote radial axonal growth, and their absence results in thin axons with severely reduced conductance velocity beyond what axon diameter predicts. This suggests glia control voltage-gated ion channel localization.
evaluation: Claims C114-C118 are supported by prior work (properly cited: Matzat et al., 2015; Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952; Kottmeier et al., 2020) and provide important context. C115 appears to be from the authors' prior work. The inference about channel control (C118) is supported by the glia ablation experiments presented in this manuscript.

result: Axonal conductance velocity depends on axial resistance (inversely correlated with diameter), membrane resistance (increased by glial wrapping), and spacing of voltage-gated ion channels.
evaluation: Claims C119-C121 represent established principles of axon physiology, properly cited to foundational and recent literature. These provide essential theoretical framework for interpreting the results.

result: Drosophila has only one voltage-gated sodium channel (Para) required for all action potentials.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2 are supported by citation to Kroll et al., 2015 and represent established knowledge about Drosophila neurobiology that provides important context.

result: In vertebrates, voltage-gated ion channel clustering occurs at nodes of Ranvier, and myelin participates in channel positioning while increasing insulation and conductance velocity.
evaluation: Claims C46-C48 represent established knowledge about vertebrate myelin, properly cited, providing comparative context for the Drosophila findings.
